medical.title: Microplastics clog liver immune cells, driving fat buildup in mice
medical.summary: Microplastics appear capable of significantly impairing the function of phagocytes in the liver, at least in mice. In turn, this disrupts the metabolism of this vital organ and increases the build-up of fat inside it. These key findings from a joint German-Austrian study led by the University of Bonn, have now been published in the journal Nature Metabolism.

medical.title: Childhood trauma doubles depression risk in adulthood, study finds
medical.summary: A recent analysis of the German National Cohort (NAKO) shows that people who experienced trauma such as abuse or neglect during their childhood or adolescence were around twice as likely to develop depression in adulthood. The links were particularly pronounced in cases of emotional abuse and neglect. The gender differences in depression appeared to be linked primarily to the fact that women were more frequently exposed to certain forms of distressing childhood experiences, rather than to a greater susceptibility of women to their psychological consequences

medical.title: Low-cost platform maps gene activity and metabolites in the same tissue sample
medical.summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) shows which genes are being expressed and where within a tissue. Spatial metabolomics (SM), on the other hand, maps the location of metabolites—small molecules produced or used by cells—within tissue.

medical.title: Anti-cancer molecules show promise in the fight against malaria
medical.summary: Molecules known for their anticancer activity have proven effective against Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes malaria. Researchers at the University of São Paulo's School of Pharmaceutical Sciences (FCF-USP) in Brazil also investigated how differences in the molecules' structure affect their impact on the parasite. The research paves the way for more effective drugs.

medical.title: High-performance AI expands electrocardiogram analysis across medical tasks
medical.summary: Conventional AI models in medicine are usually trained for a single, narrowly defined task, such as detecting a specific cardiac arrhythmia. So-called foundation models take a different approach: Much like a language model such as ChatGPT develops a comprehensive understanding of text, an ECG foundation model learns to "understand" the heart signal in all its diversity. It can then apply that knowledge to many medical questions—including those for which only limited specific training data is available. This is a decisive advantage, especially in medicine.

medical.title: Detecting diseases through body odor? New laser technology shows potential for non-invasive diagnostics
medical.summary: Researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits IIS and the Technical University of Dresden have tested a new approach for investigating disease-related changes in body odor. Using laser-based photoacoustic spectroscopy, they analyzed volatile organic compounds in simple body swabs. An initial study revealed differences between samples from healthy individuals and those from people with Parkinson's disease, COVID-19, and other diseases. The results, published in Scientific Reports, demonstrate the method's potential for faster preliminary screenings in the future.

medical.title: Kidney-sparing embolization reduces patients' risk of acute injury and death compared to surgery
medical.summary: A new study finds that embolization greatly reduces the risk of acute kidney injury and in-hospital mortality compared with nephrectomy when treating initially stable trauma patients with high-grade kidney injuries. The study was published online today in the Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology.

medical.title: Study identifies inherited genetic risk factors in childhood leukemia
medical.summary: A study from Karolinska Institutet shows that genetic testing can identify germline predisposition underlying childhood leukemia. The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help enable more personalized treatment and long-term follow-up.

medical.title: Promising therapy for fatty liver disease reduces fat, inflammation, and scarring in preclinical models
medical.summary: For millions of people living with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), treatment options remain limited. The progressive form of fatty liver disease develops when excess fat accumulates in the liver, leading to inflammation, tissue damage and fibrosis—the buildup of scar tissue that can eventually cause cirrhosis, liver failure and the need for a transplant. Although the first medications for MASH have recently become available, they are intended only for patients with advanced disease and have common side effects.

medical.title: Q&A: Earlier recognition of cerebral visual impairment in the NICU could help more children thrive
medical.summary: Mohamed El-Dib, MD, of the Division of Newborn Medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children is the corresponding author of a new study that seeks to identify and address gaps in the recognition of cerebral visual impairment (CVI) in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).

medical.title: Researchers discover overlooked process of bone renewal
medical.summary: Small tunnels in the spongy (trabecular) part of bone have been known for decades, but their role has remained unclear. Researchers from the Department of Clinical Research at the University of Southern Denmark, together with Danish and international colleagues from the U.S. and Canada, now show that these tunnels are part of a process that renews trabecular bone from within. In the hard outer layer of bone, researchers already know that similar tunnels form as part of the bone renewal process. The new study shows that a comparable process also occurs within the small rods and plates of trabecular bone. The study is published in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research.

medical.title: Prenatal exposure to depression linked to neurodevelopmental disorders
medical.summary: Children of mothers with depression had higher rates of certain neurodevelopmental disorders regardless of whether they were exposed to antidepressants in the womb, according to a new study led by Saraid McIlvride of the University of Glasgow, U.K. The study was published Sept. 29 in the journal PLOS Medicine.

medical.title: New genetic testing guidance could improve patient diagnosis worldwide
medical.summary: New guidance co-led by University of Otago researchers could help more people with suspected inherited diseases receive a clear genetic diagnosis.

medical.title: Cannabis use linked to higher risk of violence, major review finds
medical.summary: People who use cannabis are more likely both to carry out violent acts and to experience violence, according to one of the most comprehensive reviews of the evidence to date, led by researchers at King's College London.

medical.title: Aspirin did not prevent recurrence after liver metastasis surgery, study shows
medical.summary: Colon and rectal cancer often spread to the liver. In some patients, the metastases can be surgically removed or destroyed using local treatment with the aim of curing the disease. Despite this, the cancer often returns. Researchers from Karolinska Institutet wanted to investigate whether aspirin could be used as a treatment.

medical.title: About 1 in 3 Americans say RFK Jr. recommends measles vaccination
medical.summary: The number of measles cases in the United States is at its highest level in decades, a rise attributed to declining measles vaccination rates. Although U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told American parents on Aug. 2 that they should get their children vaccinated against measles, the public remains nearly evenly divided on whether he recommends the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine.

medical.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
medical.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

medical.title: Scientists thought they knew how this 70-year-old leukemia drug worked
medical.summary: A 70-year-old leukemia drug is still revealing new secrets. Researchers found that removing a protein called NUDT5 protected cells from the drug, even though simply blocking the protein had little effect. The unexpected result points to a hidden cellular role that could help explain why people respond differently to certain leukemia treatments.

medical.title: Aging muscles may be losing strength for a reason scientists missed
medical.summary: A newly identified breakdown in communication between nerves and muscles could help explain why people lose strength as they age. Researchers were able to improve muscle strength in an animal model by targeting a key protein, raising hopes that some age-related weakness could eventually be treated.

science.title: LISA to the rescue: Using light to fix cell division
science.summary: Cell division is a complex process. At the heart of this complexity is a membraneless organelle called the centrosome, which is made up of more than 200 components. It is responsible for clustering mitotic spindles, threadlike structures needed to separate genetic material. It has long remained unclear which parts of the centrosome are necessary and sufficient for spindle assembly.

science.title: Genetic audit of wheat: Researchers determine the actual variability of a gene responsible for bread quality
science.summary: A team at the University of Córdoba (UCO) has reviewed and updated the catalog of versions of the wheat gene GLU-B1, which is responsible for a protein that makes up gluten. The team has also made a collection of wheat representing the gene's true variability available to the research community.

science.title: Protein signaling cascade helps explain how plants respond to touch
science.summary: Plants cannot run away when the wind picks up, rain lashes down or a hungry herbivore begins chewing on their leaves. Instead, they must sense their surroundings and adapt. Now, researchers have uncovered an important piece of the puzzle of what happens inside plants when they are exposed to touch, injury or other physical stimuli.

science.title: New device measures curved mirrors' absolute shape to within 2 nanometers without touching them
science.summary: Researchers at AIST have developed a device that measures the absolute surface profile of curved optical elements with high precision without touching them.

science.title: AI structure prediction speeds discovery of 'molecular glues' to treat disease
science.summary: A Baylor College of Medicine-led team has developed a strategy that combines the analysis of thousands of proteins with artificial intelligence to accelerate the discovery of small molecules called molecular glues to treat disease. Their approach, published in Nature Communications, has uncovered a new class of molecular glues that could neutralize harmful proteins linked to blood cancers and autoimmune diseases. The work also shows how AI-based structural modeling can help chemists optimize compounds well before experiments reveal how they work.

science.title: New feathered, winged dinosaur from China challenges our theories on bird and dinosaur evolution
science.summary: A newly described feathered dinosaur found in northeastern China adds evidence supporting the theory that flight-related features evolved differently in various bird-like dinosaur groups. The findings, reported in Nature Communications, are based on an analysis of an exceptionally well-preserved fossil of a microraptorine (a small dinosaur with feathers and wings) found in a geological formation estimated to be between 145 and 100 million years old.

science.title: We can finally measure the damage each new coal, gas or oil project will do to people and nature
science.summary: We have long known every tonne of carbon dioxide matters to the climate. But governments keep approving new fossil fuel projects—even as climate change worsens.

science.title: A new family of materials for efficiently converting sunlight into clean energy
science.summary: Researchers at Oregon State University have developed a new family of materials that use light to produce hydrogen from water, opening the door to new ways of converting the sun's rays into clean energy.

science.title: Arctic infrastructure was built on frozen ground—drones and digital twins can help spot the permafrost thaw coming
science.summary: From the air, Wainwright, Alaska, looks like a perfectly stable band of homes and roads between the Chukchi Sea and a vast, flat tundra. But just below the surface, the frozen ground on which this town was built contains large bodies of ice. Along the eroding coastal bluffs, that hidden ice is becoming exposed and melting away.

science.title: Mysterious giant carving may show a Kushite ruler and mark an ancient borderland
science.summary: For centuries, a life-size petroglyph has stood over the rocky landscape of Miseeda in northern Sudan. Exactly who the figure carved into a granite hill represents remains uncertain, but researchers suspect it may depict an ancient Kushite ruler. In the 7th century CE, local builders constructed a Christian church directly around it.

science.title: Scientists call for protection and restoration of Africa's seagrass meadows
science.summary: A team of African researchers has published the first comprehensive review of seagrass restoration activities across Africa's coastline.

science.title: Taylor Swift: My database of her 123,553 lyrics reveals hidden patterns
science.summary: "It seems like all I ever do is change," Taylor Swift writes in the prolog to the bestselling album 1989 (Taylor's Version), released in 2023. In fact, change is a core part of the Swift marketing machine, which revolves around the evolution of her "eras."

science.title: Across six cultures, children step in when peers need help
science.summary: A new study by an international research team provides the first systematic, cross-cultural comparison of how children help their peers. While previous research has mainly focused on how children help adults, often within the family, peer interactions play an equally important but far less studied role in children's social lives across many cultures.

science.title: 8-million-year-old rhino skull found in Crete
science.summary: A rhinoceros skull at least 8 million years old has been found in the town of Sitia on Crete, the Greek news agency ANA reported Tuesday.

science.title: NASA Sets Crew-13 Launch, Docking Coverage
science.summary: NASA will provide live coverage of prelaunch, launch, and docking activities for the agency’s SpaceX Crew‑13 mission to the International Space Station. Live coverage will stream through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Crew‑13 is scheduled to launch at 11:10 a.m. EDT, Thursday, Oct. 1, from Space Launch Complex 40 at […]

science.title: Chatbots as oracles: How AI is giving new life to the ancient practice of seeking answers from inscrutable sources
science.summary: People are increasingly turning to AI for advice. A 2026 Pew report found that 10% of Americans use chatbots for emotional support or companionship. Some even find a charismatic leader in AI.

science.title: Research shows poor mental health among politicians may impair decision-making
science.summary: When political leaders disclose mental health challenges—as an increasing number of high-profile leaders have done in recent years—the public debate usually focuses on politicians' personal resilience or experiences. Yet behind these individual stories lies a far more consequential question for democracy: When elected representatives experience psychological distress, how does it alter the high-stakes choices they make on our behalf?

science.title: Suns set on hunt for giant planets in nearby binary system
science.summary: New research led by the University of Michigan is helping set the stage for future observatories to characterize rocky planets outside our solar system, planets that could prove life isn't confined to Earth. The new research represents the most sensitive modern search for giant planets in a nearby binary system—a system with two stars orbiting each other—known as 70 Ophiuchi AB, or 70 Oph AB.

science.title: Wolves did not save Yellowstone—why were we so desperate to believe they did?
science.summary: You might be among the 46 million people who've seen a video showing how wolves changed Yellowstone, or you may have heard another version of the story. Yellowstone, which covers nearly 3,500 square miles (9,100 square kilometers) of the western United States, was the world's first national park. Its pioneering reintroduction of wolves, which began in 1995, set a worldwide precedent for conservation.

science.title: SpaceX's Starship rocket does its job during first orbital flight
science.summary: SpaceX sent its Starship super-rocket on its first orbital flight—a shorter-than-planned test mission that put operational Starlink satellites into orbit for the first time.

science.title: How ocean chemistry helped life keep breathing
science.summary: Scientists have helped solve a longstanding mystery about how Earth remained habitable after oxygen first accumulated in its atmosphere more than 2 billion years ago, providing evidence that ancient ocean chemistry sustained life-friendly conditions.

science.title: Researchers find a fungus in Kentucky's forest grass that makes rare bug-fighting chemicals
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Kentucky Martin-Gatton College of Agriculture, Food and Environment (CAFE) have discovered that a fungus living inside a common Kentucky woodland grass produces a rare combination of chemicals that likely helps protect the plant from hungry insects.

science.title: Extensive audit reveals gaps between Google AI answers and cited sources
science.summary: Since its launch in 1998, Google, the world's leading search engine, has transformed how people find information online. For years, search results appeared as ranked lists of sources: Google decided what to show, but users decided what to read and whom to trust.

science.title: Plant lovers wanted: Study highlights demand for citizen science
science.summary: Over the last several years, invasive plant and insect species have found their way into more and more social media feeds. From the tree of heaven to Bradford pear trees and the ubiquitous spotted lanternfly, home gardeners are spreading the word about problematic species to their networks.

NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey […]

environment.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
environment.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

environment.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
environment.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

environment.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
environment.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

environment.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade

environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.summary: În această lună, Oceanul Atlantic a doborât un record vechi de un secol privind cea mai târzie perioadă a anului fără uragane, una dintre numeroasele consecințe ale unui fenomen El Niño istoric care a dat peste cap condițiile meteorologice globale. De obicei, în Atlanticul de Nord se înregistrează mai mult de trei uragane în această perioadă a anului. Până acum, nu a fost niciunul, scrie The Wall Street Journal.

mix_items.title: LISA to the rescue: Using light to fix cell division
mix_items.summary: Cell division is a complex process. At the heart of this complexity is a membraneless organelle called the centrosome, which is made up of more than 200 components. It is responsible for clustering mitotic spindles, threadlike structures needed to separate genetic material. It has long remained unclear which parts of the centrosome are necessary and sufficient for spindle assembly.

mix_items.title: Genetic audit of wheat: Researchers determine the actual variability of a gene responsible for bread quality
mix_items.summary: A team at the University of Córdoba (UCO) has reviewed and updated the catalog of versions of the wheat gene GLU-B1, which is responsible for a protein that makes up gluten. The team has also made a collection of wheat representing the gene's true variability available to the research community.

mix_items.title: Microplastics clog liver immune cells, driving fat buildup in mice
mix_items.summary: Microplastics appear capable of significantly impairing the function of phagocytes in the liver, at least in mice. In turn, this disrupts the metabolism of this vital organ and increases the build-up of fat inside it. These key findings from a joint German-Austrian study led by the University of Bonn, have now been published in the journal Nature Metabolism.

mix_items.title: Protein signaling cascade helps explain how plants respond to touch
mix_items.summary: Plants cannot run away when the wind picks up, rain lashes down or a hungry herbivore begins chewing on their leaves. Instead, they must sense their surroundings and adapt. Now, researchers have uncovered an important piece of the puzzle of what happens inside plants when they are exposed to touch, injury or other physical stimuli.

mix_items.title: New device measures curved mirrors' absolute shape to within 2 nanometers without touching them
mix_items.summary: Researchers at AIST have developed a device that measures the absolute surface profile of curved optical elements with high precision without touching them.

mix_items.title: Childhood trauma doubles depression risk in adulthood, study finds
mix_items.summary: A recent analysis of the German National Cohort (NAKO) shows that people who experienced trauma such as abuse or neglect during their childhood or adolescence were around twice as likely to develop depression in adulthood. The links were particularly pronounced in cases of emotional abuse and neglect. The gender differences in depression appeared to be linked primarily to the fact that women were more frequently exposed to certain forms of distressing childhood experiences, rather than to a greater susceptibility of women to their psychological consequences

mix_items.title: Low-cost platform maps gene activity and metabolites in the same tissue sample
mix_items.summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) shows which genes are being expressed and where within a tissue. Spatial metabolomics (SM), on the other hand, maps the location of metabolites—small molecules produced or used by cells—within tissue.

mix_items.title: AI structure prediction speeds discovery of 'molecular glues' to treat disease
mix_items.summary: A Baylor College of Medicine-led team has developed a strategy that combines the analysis of thousands of proteins with artificial intelligence to accelerate the discovery of small molecules called molecular glues to treat disease. Their approach, published in Nature Communications, has uncovered a new class of molecular glues that could neutralize harmful proteins linked to blood cancers and autoimmune diseases. The work also shows how AI-based structural modeling can help chemists optimize compounds well before experiments reveal how they work.

mix_items.title: New feathered, winged dinosaur from China challenges our theories on bird and dinosaur evolution
mix_items.summary: A newly described feathered dinosaur found in northeastern China adds evidence supporting the theory that flight-related features evolved differently in various bird-like dinosaur groups. The findings, reported in Nature Communications, are based on an analysis of an exceptionally well-preserved fossil of a microraptorine (a small dinosaur with feathers and wings) found in a geological formation estimated to be between 145 and 100 million years old.

mix_items.title: Anti-cancer molecules show promise in the fight against malaria
mix_items.summary: Molecules known for their anticancer activity have proven effective against Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes malaria. Researchers at the University of São Paulo's School of Pharmaceutical Sciences (FCF-USP) in Brazil also investigated how differences in the molecules' structure affect their impact on the parasite. The research paves the way for more effective drugs.

mix_items.title: We can finally measure the damage each new coal, gas or oil project will do to people and nature
mix_items.summary: We have long known every tonne of carbon dioxide matters to the climate. But governments keep approving new fossil fuel projects—even as climate change worsens.

mix_items.title: High-performance AI expands electrocardiogram analysis across medical tasks
mix_items.summary: Conventional AI models in medicine are usually trained for a single, narrowly defined task, such as detecting a specific cardiac arrhythmia. So-called foundation models take a different approach: Much like a language model such as ChatGPT develops a comprehensive understanding of text, an ECG foundation model learns to "understand" the heart signal in all its diversity. It can then apply that knowledge to many medical questions—including those for which only limited specific training data is available. This is a decisive advantage, especially in medicine.

mix_items.title: A new family of materials for efficiently converting sunlight into clean energy
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Oregon State University have developed a new family of materials that use light to produce hydrogen from water, opening the door to new ways of converting the sun's rays into clean energy.

mix_items.title: Detecting diseases through body odor? New laser technology shows potential for non-invasive diagnostics
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits IIS and the Technical University of Dresden have tested a new approach for investigating disease-related changes in body odor. Using laser-based photoacoustic spectroscopy, they analyzed volatile organic compounds in simple body swabs. An initial study revealed differences between samples from healthy individuals and those from people with Parkinson's disease, COVID-19, and other diseases. The results, published in Scientific Reports, demonstrate the method's potential for faster preliminary screenings in the future.

mix_items.title: Arctic infrastructure was built on frozen ground—drones and digital twins can help spot the permafrost thaw coming
mix_items.summary: From the air, Wainwright, Alaska, looks like a perfectly stable band of homes and roads between the Chukchi Sea and a vast, flat tundra. But just below the surface, the frozen ground on which this town was built contains large bodies of ice. Along the eroding coastal bluffs, that hidden ice is becoming exposed and melting away.

mix_items.title: Mysterious giant carving may show a Kushite ruler and mark an ancient borderland
mix_items.summary: For centuries, a life-size petroglyph has stood over the rocky landscape of Miseeda in northern Sudan. Exactly who the figure carved into a granite hill represents remains uncertain, but researchers suspect it may depict an ancient Kushite ruler. In the 7th century CE, local builders constructed a Christian church directly around it.

mix_items.title: Scientists call for protection and restoration of Africa's seagrass meadows
mix_items.summary: A team of African researchers has published the first comprehensive review of seagrass restoration activities across Africa's coastline.

mix_items.title: Taylor Swift: My database of her 123,553 lyrics reveals hidden patterns
mix_items.summary: "It seems like all I ever do is change," Taylor Swift writes in the prolog to the bestselling album 1989 (Taylor's Version), released in 2023. In fact, change is a core part of the Swift marketing machine, which revolves around the evolution of her "eras."

mix_items.title: Kidney-sparing embolization reduces patients' risk of acute injury and death compared to surgery
mix_items.summary: A new study finds that embolization greatly reduces the risk of acute kidney injury and in-hospital mortality compared with nephrectomy when treating initially stable trauma patients with high-grade kidney injuries. The study was published online today in the Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology.

mix_items.title: Across six cultures, children step in when peers need help
mix_items.summary: A new study by an international research team provides the first systematic, cross-cultural comparison of how children help their peers. While previous research has mainly focused on how children help adults, often within the family, peer interactions play an equally important but far less studied role in children's social lives across many cultures.

mix_items.title: Study identifies inherited genetic risk factors in childhood leukemia
mix_items.summary: A study from Karolinska Institutet shows that genetic testing can identify germline predisposition underlying childhood leukemia. The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help enable more personalized treatment and long-term follow-up.

mix_items.title: 8-million-year-old rhino skull found in Crete
mix_items.summary: A rhinoceros skull at least 8 million years old has been found in the town of Sitia on Crete, the Greek news agency ANA reported Tuesday.

mix_items.title: NASA Sets Crew-13 Launch, Docking Coverage
mix_items.summary: NASA will provide live coverage of prelaunch, launch, and docking activities for the agency’s SpaceX Crew‑13 mission to the International Space Station. Live coverage will stream through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Crew‑13 is scheduled to launch at 11:10 a.m. EDT, Thursday, Oct. 1, from Space Launch Complex 40 at […]

mix_items.title: Chatbots as oracles: How AI is giving new life to the ancient practice of seeking answers from inscrutable sources
mix_items.summary: People are increasingly turning to AI for advice. A 2026 Pew report found that 10% of Americans use chatbots for emotional support or companionship. Some even find a charismatic leader in AI.

mix_items.title: Promising therapy for fatty liver disease reduces fat, inflammation, and scarring in preclinical models
mix_items.summary: For millions of people living with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), treatment options remain limited. The progressive form of fatty liver disease develops when excess fat accumulates in the liver, leading to inflammation, tissue damage and fibrosis—the buildup of scar tissue that can eventually cause cirrhosis, liver failure and the need for a transplant. Although the first medications for MASH have recently become available, they are intended only for patients with advanced disease and have common side effects.

mix_items.title: Research shows poor mental health among politicians may impair decision-making
mix_items.summary: When political leaders disclose mental health challenges—as an increasing number of high-profile leaders have done in recent years—the public debate usually focuses on politicians' personal resilience or experiences. Yet behind these individual stories lies a far more consequential question for democracy: When elected representatives experience psychological distress, how does it alter the high-stakes choices they make on our behalf?

mix_items.title: Q&A: Earlier recognition of cerebral visual impairment in the NICU could help more children thrive
mix_items.summary: Mohamed El-Dib, MD, of the Division of Newborn Medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children is the corresponding author of a new study that seeks to identify and address gaps in the recognition of cerebral visual impairment (CVI) in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).

mix_items.title: Suns set on hunt for giant planets in nearby binary system
mix_items.summary: New research led by the University of Michigan is helping set the stage for future observatories to characterize rocky planets outside our solar system, planets that could prove life isn't confined to Earth. The new research represents the most sensitive modern search for giant planets in a nearby binary system—a system with two stars orbiting each other—known as 70 Ophiuchi AB, or 70 Oph AB.

mix_items.title: Wolves did not save Yellowstone—why were we so desperate to believe they did?
mix_items.summary: You might be among the 46 million people who've seen a video showing how wolves changed Yellowstone, or you may have heard another version of the story. Yellowstone, which covers nearly 3,500 square miles (9,100 square kilometers) of the western United States, was the world's first national park. Its pioneering reintroduction of wolves, which began in 1995, set a worldwide precedent for conservation.

mix_items.title: Researchers discover overlooked process of bone renewal
mix_items.summary: Small tunnels in the spongy (trabecular) part of bone have been known for decades, but their role has remained unclear. Researchers from the Department of Clinical Research at the University of Southern Denmark, together with Danish and international colleagues from the U.S. and Canada, now show that these tunnels are part of a process that renews trabecular bone from within. In the hard outer layer of bone, researchers already know that similar tunnels form as part of the bone renewal process. The new study shows that a comparable process also occurs within the small rods and plates of trabecular bone. The study is published in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research.

mix_items.title: Prenatal exposure to depression linked to neurodevelopmental disorders
mix_items.summary: Children of mothers with depression had higher rates of certain neurodevelopmental disorders regardless of whether they were exposed to antidepressants in the womb, according to a new study led by Saraid McIlvride of the University of Glasgow, U.K. The study was published Sept. 29 in the journal PLOS Medicine.

mix_items.title: SpaceX's Starship rocket does its job during first orbital flight
mix_items.summary: SpaceX sent its Starship super-rocket on its first orbital flight—a shorter-than-planned test mission that put operational Starlink satellites into orbit for the first time.

mix_items.title: How ocean chemistry helped life keep breathing
mix_items.summary: Scientists have helped solve a longstanding mystery about how Earth remained habitable after oxygen first accumulated in its atmosphere more than 2 billion years ago, providing evidence that ancient ocean chemistry sustained life-friendly conditions.

mix_items.title: New genetic testing guidance could improve patient diagnosis worldwide
mix_items.summary: New guidance co-led by University of Otago researchers could help more people with suspected inherited diseases receive a clear genetic diagnosis.

mix_items.title: Researchers find a fungus in Kentucky's forest grass that makes rare bug-fighting chemicals
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Kentucky Martin-Gatton College of Agriculture, Food and Environment (CAFE) have discovered that a fungus living inside a common Kentucky woodland grass produces a rare combination of chemicals that likely helps protect the plant from hungry insects.

mix_items.title: Cannabis use linked to higher risk of violence, major review finds
mix_items.summary: People who use cannabis are more likely both to carry out violent acts and to experience violence, according to one of the most comprehensive reviews of the evidence to date, led by researchers at King's College London.

mix_items.title: Extensive audit reveals gaps between Google AI answers and cited sources
mix_items.summary: Since its launch in 1998, Google, the world's leading search engine, has transformed how people find information online. For years, search results appeared as ranked lists of sources: Google decided what to show, but users decided what to read and whom to trust.

mix_items.title: Plant lovers wanted: Study highlights demand for citizen science
mix_items.summary: Over the last several years, invasive plant and insect species have found their way into more and more social media feeds. From the tree of heaven to Bradford pear trees and the ubiquitous spotted lanternfly, home gardeners are spreading the word about problematic species to their networks.

mix_items.title: Aspirin did not prevent recurrence after liver metastasis surgery, study shows
mix_items.summary: Colon and rectal cancer often spread to the liver. In some patients, the metastases can be surgically removed or destroyed using local treatment with the aim of curing the disease. Despite this, the cancer often returns. Researchers from Karolinska Institutet wanted to investigate whether aspirin could be used as a treatment.

mix_items.title: About 1 in 3 Americans say RFK Jr. recommends measles vaccination
mix_items.summary: The number of measles cases in the United States is at its highest level in decades, a rise attributed to declining measles vaccination rates. Although U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told American parents on Aug. 2 that they should get their children vaccinated against measles, the public remains nearly evenly divided on whether he recommends the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine.

mix_items.title: Crew-13 Rocket and Spacecraft at Launch Pad
mix_items.summary: Ahead of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission launch, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft are vertical at the launch pad of Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida in this Sept. 27, 2026, photo. NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey […]

mix_items.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
mix_items.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

mix_items.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
mix_items.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

mix_items.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
mix_items.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

mix_items.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

mix_items.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
mix_items.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

mix_items.title: Scientists thought they knew how this 70-year-old leukemia drug worked
mix_items.summary: A 70-year-old leukemia drug is still revealing new secrets. Researchers found that removing a protein called NUDT5 protected cells from the drug, even though simply blocking the protein had little effect. The unexpected result points to a hidden cellular role that could help explain why people respond differently to certain leukemia treatments.

mix_items.title: Aging muscles may be losing strength for a reason scientists missed
mix_items.summary: A newly identified breakdown in communication between nerves and muscles could help explain why people lose strength as they age. Researchers were able to improve muscle strength in an animal model by targeting a key protein, raising hopes that some age-related weakness could eventually be treated.

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific
mix_items.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .
